title: Ibn Zuhr tests surgery on a goat

confidence.note: The goat experiment is known only from Ibn Zuhr's own account in the *Taysir*, which is undated; it was composed late in his life, sometime before his death in 1162 (Al-Rubaye puts it between 1121 and 1162). The experiment itself dates from his training, earlier still. His birth year is estimated at 1091–1095 by modern scholars. The story rests on his own report alone.

people: Abu Marwan Ibn Zuhr, 'Avenzoar' (c. 1092–1162), physician of Seville
Abd al-Mu'min, Almohad ruler to whom the *Taysir* was dedicated
Ibn Rushd, 'Averroes', philosopher-physician of Córdoba, about thirty years younger, who admired the *Taysir*
summary: Having read the quarrel over whether a cut windpipe could be survived, a 12th-century Seville physician, by his own account, tried it on a goat first.
body: Surgeons had argued for centuries over whether opening the windpipe of a choking patient was safe. In the *Taysir*, his manual of treatments and diets, the Seville physician Abu Marwan Ibn Zuhr (Avenzoar) recalls testing it in training: he cut into a goat's windpipe, cut away a patch of it just smaller than a lupine seed, and washed the wound with water and honey until the animal recovered and lived a long time. The book, dedicated to the Almohad ruler Abd al-Mu'min, was called the finest work of its day on experience-based medicine by Ibn Rushd (Averroes). It also set apart a parasitic form of scabies.

links.note: Al-Razi had earlier tested mercury on monkeys before giving it to people.
Al-Zahrawi had already judged a cut windpipe survivable from a human case.

title: Maimonides the physician

confidence.note: His medical works survive and are well studied; most were written in the last two decades of his life, though individual treatises are not all precisely dated. Even his birth year is given as 1135 or 1138 by different scholars.

people: Moses Maimonides (1138–1204; some sources 1135), rabbi, philosopher and physician
al-Qadi al-Fadil, chief official of Sultan Saladin and his patron
al-Malik al-Afdal, son of Saladin and his later patient
summary: The greatest rabbi of his age made his living as a court doctor in Cairo, writing advice on asthma, diet and sex for wealthy Muslim patients.
body: Moses Maimonides, the leading rabbinic authority of his time, settled in Fustat (Old Cairo) and earned his living as a physician. He served al-Qadi al-Fadil, the top official of Sultan Saladin, and later Saladin's son al-Malik al-Afdal. Most of his ten medical books date from the last two decades of his life: short pieces of advice for wealthy Muslim patients on asthma, hemorrhoids and sex, a health regimen, written for al-Afdal in 1198, that stresses moderate diet, exercise and clean air, and a large anthology of aphorisms drawn from Hippocrates and Galen, whose views he respected but did not accept wholesale.

myth.record: Some modern writers say so flatly, but the patrons that the biographical sources used here name are Saladin's chief official, al-Qadi al-Fadil, and later Saladin's son al-Afdal. None of them records him treating Saladin himself.

links.note: Galen was the authority he cited most, and argued with.
Ibn Zuhr was among the Muslim physicians he quoted often.

title: Ibn al-Nafis and the pulmonary circulation

confidence.note: The commentary survives in manuscript and its argument is not in doubt. Its date rests on modern accounts that he wrote it at 29, which depends on a birth year given as 1210 or 1213 (the range runs from his arrival in Cairo in 1236 to his death in 1288). Whether Servetus or Colombo knew his work is disputed: one encyclopedia holds that a Latin translator knew of it, while others find no evidence that the passage reached Europe.

people: Ibn al-Nafis (c. 1213–1288), physician of Damascus and Cairo
Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi, Egyptian physician who found the manuscript in Berlin in 1924
Max Meyerhof, medical orientalist in Cairo who publicized and translated it
summary: Three centuries before Europe, a Cairo physician declared Galen wrong: blood cannot seep through the heart's wall, so it must pass through the lungs.
body: Galen taught that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores in the wall between the ventricles. In his commentary on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's *Canon*, the Damascus-trained physician Ibn al-Nafis flatly denied it: the wall is solid and has no passage, visible or invisible. Blood must therefore travel from the right ventricle through the lungs and reach the left side from there. He even inferred small passages between the pulmonary artery and vein, some 400 years before Malpighi saw capillaries.

Ibn al-Nafis became personal physician to Sultan Baybars and head of the physicians of Egypt and Syria, and left his house and library to the Mansuri hospital in Cairo. His insight lay unnoticed by modern scholars until 1924, when the Egyptian physician Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi found a manuscript in Berlin while writing a doctoral thesis for Freiburg.

Michael Servetus in 1553 and Realdo Colombo in 1559 described the same route. A Latin translation of another of Ibn al-Nafis's works appeared in 1547, and one encyclopedia holds that its translator knew of the discovery, but many historians think the Europeans reached the idea independently.

myth.tradition: Servetus and Colombo copied the pulmonary circulation from Ibn al-Nafis through Latin translations.
myth.record: No Latin version of his passage on the lungs is documented in the sources consulted; the 1547 translation by Andrea Alpago dealt with compound drugs and apparently did not mention the lung route. Transmission remains possible but unproven.

links.note: His discovery appears in a commentary on the anatomy of the *Canon*.
He rejected Galen's invisible pores in the heart's septum.
Harvey later set the lung route inside a full circulation.
He bequeathed his house and library to the hospital.

title: The Mansuri hospital of Cairo

confidence.note: Northrup dates the founding to 683/1284 (a Hijri year that runs into 1285) and two founding endowment deeds survive, though the one she cites is dated April 1286. What daily life was like rests on those deeds and on later chroniclers such as al-Nuwayri and al-Maqrizi.

people: al-Mansur Qalawun, Mamluk sultan and founder
summary: A Mamluk sultan's hospital, founded in 1284, gave patients money and clothing when they went home, and an eye clinic still stands on the same site.
body: In 1284 the Mamluk sultan Qalawun founded a hospital beside his tomb and madrasa in central Cairo; one account says he vowed to build it after being treated with medicines from Nur al-Din's hospital in Damascus. According to the chronicler al-Maqrizi, the sultan paid male and female attendants, and patients were housed by condition, with rooms for eye cases, surgery and women. Discharged patients received money and clothing. Christians and Jews were barred. By 1798 the building had fallen into disrepair; an eye clinic opened on the site in 1915.

myth.tradition: The Mansuri hospital welcomed patients of every faith.
myth.record: Its founding deed, as historian Linda Northrup reads it, barred Christians and Jews from treatment and employment there, which she calls apparently a new development, though Christian and Jewish doctors still served at the sultan's court.

links.note: It followed the model of earlier hospitals such as Nur al-Din's in Damascus.
Ibn al-Nafis left his house and library to it.

title: Andalusian physicians argue the plague is contagious

confidence.note: Ibn Khatima wrote during the epidemic at Almería, which began in June 1348; one recent study cites his treatise as 1349. Ibn al-Khatib's treatise concerns the same plague, but its exact date is less certain, so the range runs to his death in 1374. Ibn Khatima's birth year is disputed (c. 1324 in some studies, before 1300 in others).

place: Almería and Granada, Nasrid kingdom of Granada (Spain)
people: Ibn Khatima (d. 1369), physician and poet of Almería
Lisan al-Din Ibn al-Khatib (1313–1374), vizier of Granada, historian and his student
summary: As the Black Death swept Spain, two Muslim scholars argued, despite a famous saying of the Prophet, that plague passes from person to person.
body: In Almería, where plague raged from June 1348 into the winter of 1349, the physician Ibn Khatima wrote a treatise in ten questions. He observed that those who nursed the sick fell ill with the same symptoms, and that dealers selling the clothes of the dead spread the disease. His student and friend Ibn al-Khatib, soon vizier of Granada, argued in his own treatise that contagion was proved by experience and observation. Ibn Khatima gave the last four of his ten questions to religious texts, including how to reconcile the evidence with the Prophet's saying 'no contagion'. Ibn al-Khatib called ignoring the proofs an affront to God.

myth.tradition: These Andalusian writers anticipated germ theory.
myth.record: They still traced plague to corrupted air; for Ibn Khatima, contagion meant the sick passing that corruption on through breath, contact and clothing.

links.note: The same pandemic, seen from Christian Europe.

title: Mansur's illustrated anatomy

confidence.note: The treatise is dedicated to a Pir Muhammad, most likely Timur's grandson who ruled Fars from 1394 to 1409, which would date it to those years, while the National Library of Medicine gives c. 1390 and 'the end of the 14th century'. No copy from the author's lifetime survives: the earliest dated one is from 1488.

people: Mansur ibn Ilyas (fl. c. 1390), physician of a Shiraz family of scholars
Pir Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Timur, ruler of Fars 1394–1409, probable dedicatee
summary: The earliest full-body anatomical pictures known from the Islamic world: five squatting figures for bones, nerves, muscles, veins and arteries.
body: No pictures of the entire human body survive from the Islamic world before those in a short Persian treatise by Mansur ibn Ilyas of Shiraz, dedicated to a Pir Muhammad, most likely Timur's grandson. Five full-page figures in a squatting posture show the bones, nerves, muscles, veins and arteries, with labels in Arabic and Persian; a sixth shows a pregnant woman. Mansur did not invent the series. Strikingly similar Latin figures go back to the 12th century, and how the set reached Persia is unknown. The oldest dated copy was made in Isfahan in 1488.

myth.tradition: Mansur ibn Ilyas drew the first full-body anatomical figures.
myth.record: His are the earliest preserved from the Islamic world, but most of his figures were not original: a closely similar series of full-length figures appears in early Latin manuscripts, the earliest from the 12th century.

links.note: Its small skull and jaw diagrams also appear in copies of the *Canon*.
A century and a half later, anatomical figures drawn from dissection.

title: Sabuncuoğlu's illustrated surgery

confidence.note: The author dates the work to 870 AH (1465) and gives his age in it; three manuscripts survive, one apparently in his own hand. Reading some painted women as physicians rests on marginal labels such as *suret-i tabibe*; sources differ slightly on his age in the book (80 or 83) and on whether he painted the miniatures himself.

people: Şerefeddin Sabuncuoğlu (c. 1386–after 1468), surgeon of the Amasya hospital
Mehmed II (r. 1444–46, 1451–81), Ottoman sultan to whom he presented the book
summary: An Ottoman surgeon in his eighties wrote a Turkish surgical manual with 140 miniatures, including some of women physicians at work.
body: In 1465, in his eighties and after 14 years practicing at the hospital of Amasya, Şerefeddin Sabuncuoğlu finished a surgical manual in plain Turkish, saying it would let more people benefit, and went to Istanbul to present it to Sultan Mehmed II. The *Cerrahiyye-i İlhaniyye* translates the last three surgical books of al-Zahrawi's *Tasrif* and adds new sections. Where al-Zahrawi pictured only instruments, Sabuncuoğlu added miniatures showing how to use them, 140 in all. In some, a woman labeled *tabibe*, a female physician, treats a patient.

links.note: Most of the text translates the surgical part of al-Zahrawi's *Tasrif*.
